content: There is no mention of loss to follow-up or details provided regarding the participation rate of eligible participants. Additionally, the study has a small sample size, and no information is provided about the baseline characteristics of the study sample. In Bjelland 2013, the research question or objective was clearly stated. However, the study population was not clearly specified or defined. The exposure measures were not clearly defined, valid, reliable, or implemented consistently across all study participants. The participation rate of eligible persons was less than 50%. The exposure(s) were assessed more than once over time. It is unclear whether all subjects were selected or recruited from the same or similar populations, including the same time period. The inclusion and exclusion criteria for study participation were not uniformly prescribed or applied to all participants. The outcome measures (dependent variables) were not clearly defined, valid, reliable, or implemented consistently across all study participants. There was no justification for the sample size, no power description, and no variance or effect estimates provided. The outcome assessors were not blinded to the exposure status of participants. The exposure(s) of interest were measured prior to the outcome(s) being measured. The loss to follow-up after baseline exceeded 20%. The timeframe was sufficient to reasonably expect an association between exposure and outcome if one existed. However, key potential confounding variables were not measured or statistically adjusted for their impact on the relationship between exposure(s) and outcome(s). Overall, the study was rated as poor in quality and lacked internal validity. It is difficult to determine whether information bias occurred due to missing methods and details in the report. For example, the study population, exposure measures, and outcome measures were never clearly defined. Furthermore, the study did not account for any confounding variables, and measurement bias may have occurred. The results should be interpreted with caution. In Chang 2007, the research question or objective was clearly stated. However, the study population was not clearly specified or defined. The exposure measures were not clearly defined, valid, reliable, or implemented consistently across all study participants. It is unclear whether the participation rate of eligible persons was at least 50%. The exposure(s) were not assessed more than once over time. It is unclear whether all subjects were selected or recruited from the same or similar populations, including the same time period. The inclusion and exclusion criteria for study participation were not uniformly prescribed or applied to all participants. The outcome measures (dependent variables) were not clearly defined, valid, reliable, or implemented consistently across all study participants. There was no justification for the sample size, no power description, and no variance or effect estimates provided. It is unclear whether the outcome assessors were blinded to the exposure status of participants. It is also unclear whether the exposure(s) of interest were measured prior to the outcome(s) being measured. It is unclear whether the loss to follow-up after baseline was 20% or less. The timeframe was not applicable to reasonably expect an association between exposure and outcome. Key potential confounding variables were not measured or statistically adjusted for their impact on the relationship between exposure(s) and outcome(s). Overall, the study was rated as poor in quality and lacked internal validity. The paper does not include a methods section, and therefore no details are provided on the tools used to measure the exposure or outcome. The sample size is not clearly stated and had to be inferred from tables. In the analysis, the reference arm is not reported within the tables, requiring the reader to infer this information from the text. The results should be interpreted with extreme caution.
